counterfactual_missing_items: No documented coronary spasm provocation test
No documented response to nitrates or calcium-channel blockers
No echocardiographic evidence to exclude structural cardiomyopathy or HCM
decisive_items: ST segments elevated 4-6 mm in leads II, III and aVF, with ST depression in leads V2-V6
Widespread ST-segment elevations (4-15 mm) in leads II, III, aVF, and V2-V6
10% stenosis in proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD) and right coronary artery (RCA)
response.rationale: R2 best explains transient widespread ST-segment elevations with non-obstructive coronary arteries and alcohol-triggered syncope/arrhythmias as vasospastic angina. R3 captures alcohol-related arrhythmias but not the ischemic ST-elevation pattern; R4 and R5 lack structural/functional evidence; R1 and C1 only describe an ECG finding rather than the underlying diagnosis.

rejected.why: Explains alcohol-provoked VT and syncope but does not account for widespread ST-segment elevations or non-obstructive angiography; arrhythmia is a consequence rather than the primary diagnosis.
No heart failure, structural, or echocardiographic evidence; normal troponin and transient episodes are not consistent with alcoholic cardiomyopathy.
Describes an ECG finding rather than a unifying diagnosis; the AV block is better explained by ischemia or vasospasm.
Same limitation as R1; only appends 'high-degree' without adding a diagnostic mechanism.
No echocardiographic evidence of hypertrophy or obstruction; the ECG and angiographic findings are more consistent with coronary vasospasm.
